chunks: Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abu al-Mi'za from Abu Basir said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: A gift (hiba) is valid whether it has been taken possession of or not, whether it has been divided or not. And for honey (nahln), that is not valid until it is taken possession of. The people intended that [distinction] and thus erred. The meaning in these narrations is a type of preference (istihbab) rather than obligation (wujub). Furthermore, the latter report included a distinction between honey and a gift, and we have clarified that there is no difference between them. It is permissible that it emerged as a form of precautionary piety (taqiyyah), because it is the view of some of the Sunni Muslims. And what we mentioned is for clarification.

key_terms.النَّحْلُ: Honey (specifically referring to the produce of bees)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the validity of a gift (hiba) and honey (nahln) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the validity of a gift (hiba), which is effective upon agreement regardless of possession, and honey (nahln), which requires actual possession. He attributes the discrepancy in narrations to either popular misunderstanding or taqiyyah, noting that the general public often conflates the two, while the Shia position emphasizes the immediate validity of hiba. This ruling highlights the jurisprudential nuance between contractual consent and physical transfer in Islamic law.
